## What it does

Point it at a plate ID. It reads the experimental layout from the plate's
metadata, corrects illumination, and segments every nucleus and cell with
[Cellpose](https://www.cellpose.org/). It measures them, assigns each cell a
cell-cycle phase from DNA content and EdU signal, and attaches the results back
to OMERO. A trained CNN classifies cell features, and
[Trackastra](https://github.com/weigertlab/trackastra) follows lineages through
live-cell timelapses.

::: {.fig-card}
![**The OMERO-Screen platform.** Images and plate metadata enter from the microscope. The core pipeline handles metadata parsing, flatfield correction, segmentation, classification and feature extraction, with a separate cyclic-IF route for registration and feature alignment. omero-utils brokers every exchange with the OMERO server, which stores plates, masks, metadata and feature data. Single-cell measurements land in the local cellview DuckDB database, feeding the napari viewers, cellclass classifier training, and the plotting package.](../assets/figure1-architecture.png){#fig-architecture}
:::

```bash
omero-screen 1234 --stitch          # segment a plate, write results back to OMERO
cellview import plate 1234          # pull the measurements into a local database
```

Two commands: analyse the plate, then pull the measurements into a local
database you can query, plot and classify.

## The journey

Six steps, each with a guide. You do not need to know which Python package owns
which step.

| | Step | You run | Guide |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Connect** to an OMERO server and check your plate's metadata | `omero-screen --help` | [Install & configure](installation.qmd) |
| 2 | **Analyse** a plate — segment, measure, assign cell-cycle phase | `omero-screen <plate_id>` | [Your first plate](first-plate.qmd) |
| 3 | **Inspect** segmentation quality and browse cells interactively | napari widgets | [Napari](../napari/) |
| 4 | **Store & query** single-cell measurements locally | `cellview import plate` | [CellView](../cellview/) |
| 5 | **Classify** cell features with a trained CNN | `cellclass train` | [CellClass](../cellclass/) |
| 6 | **Plot** publication-ready statistics | Python API | [Plots](../plots/) |

## Inside one analysis run

::: {.fig-card}
![Starting from a plate ID, the pipeline parses experimental metadata, builds per-channel flatfield masks, then iterates over every non-empty well. Each image is segmented with Cellpose, features are extracted with `regionprops`, and results are written back to OMERO as CSV attachments. Cell-cycle assignment and optional classification run once all wells are done.](../assets/analysis-loop.svg){#fig-loop width=85%}
:::

Two things are worth knowing early:

- **Stitched mode** (`--stitch`) segments the whole well as one canvas instead of
  field by field, so a cell straddling two fields is no longer cut in half by
  the border filter on each side.
- **Live-cell tracking** (`--track`) relabels nuclei with a stable `track_id`
  across timepoints using [Trackastra](https://github.com/weigertlab/trackastra),
  giving you lineages rather than independent snapshots.

## Why the results are reproducible

Every number in a figure traces back to a plate ID, a segmentation mask stored
in OMERO, and a row in a local database. Re-running a plate reproduces it;
sharing it means sharing an ID rather than a folder. The analysis stops being
something that happened once, on one desktop, in a way nobody can retrace.

## The packages

Each has its own reference site with generated API and CLI documentation.

| Package | What it is |
|---|---|
| **omero-screen** | The analysis pipeline: Cellpose segmentation, feature extraction, cell-cycle phases, flatfield correction, stitching, tracking |
| **[cellview](../cellview/)** | DuckDB-backed single-cell database with a CLI and a Python API |
| **[omero-screen-plots](../plots/)** | Statistical plots built for publication figures — cell cycle, counts, features, classification, synergy |
| **[omero-screen-napari](../napari/)** | Napari widgets for browsing plates, inspecting galleries and labelling CNN training data |
| **[cellclass](../cellclass/)** | CNN classifier training, sweeps and inference for cell features |
| **[omero-utils](../utils/)** | Connection handling, attachments, map annotations and image I/O against the OMERO API |

## Performance and accuracy

The pipeline has been benchmarked across CPU, Apple silicon (MPS) and two
NVIDIA GPUs, for both Cellpose 3 and Cellpose 4 models.

::: {.fig-card}
![**Benchmarking the pipeline.** (**A**) Pre-processing and the analysis loop around the OMERO server. (**B**, **C**) Per-image processing time and how it divides between download, nucleus segmentation, cell segmentation and feature extraction. (**D**) Total pipeline run time across CPU, MPS, an NVIDIA A40 and an RTX 5090. (**E**) Boundary accuracy against manual annotation, per object, for nuclei and cells. (**F**) Detection accuracy as average precision across IoU matching thresholds.](../assets/figure2-benchmarks.png){#fig-benchmarks}
:::

Two practical conclusions: download time dominates on fast GPUs, so the image
cache matters more than raw compute once you have one; and Cellpose 4 is
markedly more accurate on cell boundaries, which is why it is worth an NVIDIA
GPU if you have access to one.
